notes: Missing-trader VAT fraud appeal; extension refused and six-and-a-half-year sentence upheld.

enrichment.short_title: El-Heri: missing-trader VAT fraud conviction and sentence appeal dismissed
key_facts: Ahmed El-Heri was convicted after a seven-month trial of conspiracy to evade VAT in a missing-trader fraud involving computer chips imported from EU suppliers through phantom companies.
Customs raids in July 2000 uncovered documents at the appellant's premises linking him to multiple bogus importing and middleman companies in the fraud chain.
The revenue loss was about £8 million; the appellant was sentenced to six-and-a-half years, the same term as co-conspirator Newman.
The appellant sought an extension of time to appeal conviction on fresh allegations about co-conspirator Wim Coene and Customs informant misconduct, which the court rejected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for extension of time to appeal against conviction following Single Judge refusal, together with appeal against sentence with leave.
enrichment.outcome: Extension application refused; sentence appeal dismissed; six-and-a-half-year imprisonment held not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: On a missing-trader VAT conspiracy each conspirator answers for the whole fraud and loss; a sentence at the top of the bracket for a £6–8 million sophisticated fraud involving the appellant's son is not manifestly excessive, and unevidenced allegations about informants do not justify reopening conviction.
legal_issues: Whether extension of time to appeal conviction should be granted on alleged Customs informant misconduct
Whether Wim Coene and Anthony Watkins-Burton were the same person
Whether the sentence was manifestly excessive compared with co-conspirator Newman
Whether VAT loss should be apportioned between different bogus companies
linked_authorities: R v Dosanjh [1999] 1 Cr App R 107

confidence.notes: Background, aggravating factors and dual disposals on conviction application and sentence are clearly recorded.

notes: Section 459 strike-out; all unfair prejudice heads held to have no real prospect of success.

enrichment.short_title: Hough v Hardcastle: section 459 petition struck out on Texas Embassy restaurant shares
key_facts: Minority Class C shareholders in Grandactual Limited, operator of the Texas Embassy restaurant in Cockspur Street, petitioned under section 459 alleging unfair prejudice by the Hough family developers.

Complaints included unauthorised issue of additional C shares without class consent, mismatch between articles and shareholders agreement on redemption price, and differential treatment of related Isle of Man licensor Injebreck Limited.
The petitioners had participated in or acquiesced in some challenged conduct years earlier and refused to cooperate with proposed articles amendments needed to redeem C shares at paid-in value.
Sir Donald Rattee struck out or dismissed the petition on summary judgment grounds under CPR 3.4 and 24.2.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to strike out or dismiss a section 459 unfair prejudice petition for disclosing no real prospect of success.
enrichment.outcome: Petition struck out or dismissed; none of the four heads of alleged unfairly prejudicial conduct had any real prospect of resulting in section 461 relief.
enrichment.ratio: Relief under section 461 is discretionary and the court should not entertain stale section 459 complaints about conduct in which petitioners participated without protest; conduct of an associated Isle of Man licensing company is not conduct of the operating company's affairs unless control principles from Nicholas and Citybranch apply, which they did not here.
legal_issues: Whether delayed challenge to unauthorised C share issues could succeed under section 459
Whether affairs of Injebreck Limited could constitute affairs of Grandactual Limited
Whether licensing fee payments to Injebreck were unfairly prejudicial
Whether article 11 class consent requirements invalidated share issues
linked_authorities: Nicholas v Soundcraft Electronics Limited [1993] BCLC 360
Re Citybranch Group Limited [2004] 4 All ER 735
Re A Company No 001761 of 1986 [1987] BCLC 141

confidence.notes: Each allegation is addressed separately with explicit strike-out reasoning though some valuation issues remain for trial if petition had survived.

notes: Secure tenancy succession appeal; tolerated trespasser status upheld, no new tenancy found.

enrichment.short_title: Newham v Hawkins: no secure tenancy succession for tolerated trespasser's family
key_facts: Mrs Margaret Hawkins became successor tenant of a Newham secure tenancy on her husband's death but breached a suspended possession order for rent arrears in 1991 and thereafter remained as a tolerated trespasser.
After arrears were cleared the council treated her account as a tenant but did not grant new terms or discharge the possession order under section 85(4).
On Mrs Hawkins' death in 1998 her sons and grandson claimed succession under section 87, which is unavailable where the deceased was herself a successor.
The county court judge held no new secure tenancy had been created by the council's forbearance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Bow County Court possession order rejecting section 87 succession to a secure tenancy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Mrs Hawkins remained either a tolerated trespasser or occupier under her original successor tenancy, so the appellants could not succeed to the tenancy.
enrichment.ratio: In the absence of special circumstances, a landlord's agreement not to enforce a possession order after breach of suspension does not create a new secure tenancy; forbearance while arrears are paid relates to occupation under the terminated tenancy in limbo revivable under section 85, following Burrows v Brent.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Hawkins acquired a new secure tenancy after clearing arrears
Whether section 85(4) discharge was available after breach of suspended order
Whether council letters and fresh possession procedures implied a new tenancy
Whether section 87 succession was barred because Mrs Hawkins was a successor tenant
linked_authorities: Burrows v Brent London Borough Council [1996] 1 WLR 1448
Swindon BC v Aston [2003] HLR 610
Marshall v Bradford MDC [2001] HLR 428
Thompson v Elmbridge [1987] 1 WLR 1425

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, undisputed facts and application of Burrows are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Case stated on assaulting police; acquittal quashed for irrational fact finding and section 35 misuse.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Kavanagh: head-butt acquittal remitted after irrational magistrates' findings

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Sean Kavanagh was acquitted at Ealing magistrates' court of assaulting PC Hayward by deliberate head-butt during a domestic disturbance arrest at his home.
Two police officers gave clear evidence of a deliberate head-butt during a struggle on the landing; the defendant did not give evidence.
Magistrates found the contact accidental, declined to draw adverse inferences under section 35 because the defendant seemed depressed, and criticised police zeal.
The DPP appealed by case stated questioning the rationality of those findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal of assaulting a police constable in execution of duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a fresh bench or district judge; magistrates were not entitled to find positively that the head-butt was not deliberate on the prosecution evidence accepted as clear.
enrichment.ratio: A submission that a defendant may not give evidence is not an evidential basis under section 35(1)(b); where prosecution evidence clearly establishes deliberate assault, magistrates cannot rationally find accidental contact without rejecting that evidence, and failure to draw proper inferences from silence may also vitiate the verdict.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates could find accidental contact while accepting clear police evidence of deliberate head-butt
Whether section 35 adverse inference from silence was properly excluded
Whether depression evidence justified not drawing inferences under section 35(1)(b)
Whether PC Hayward was acting in execution of duty
linked_authorities: R v Cowan [1996] QB 373

confidence.notes: Case stated questions and High Court answers on each ground are explicit.

notes: Foot-and-mouth C&D contract trial; illegality and sham defences rejected, contractual and negligence claims largely upheld on liability.

enrichment.short_title: Hill v Defra: foot-and-mouth cleansing contracts enforceable despite bankrupt farmer's role
key_facts: About 2,000 sheep and 160 cattle at Lower Dunscombe Farm were slaughtered in April 2001 on mistaken foot-and-mouth suspicion; Defra contracted with NCF Limited for cleansing and disinfection work performed largely by undischarged bankrupt Mr Hill.
Defra refused payment relying on illegality under CDDA section 11, sham agreements, and disputed timesheets and plant hire.
Mr Hill had structured farming through NCF after bankruptcy using Clifton nominees; the trustee had assigned tenancies back to him.
Claims included labour and plant under two C&D agreements, polytunnel and gate damage in negligence, and compensation for destroyed feed under section 36.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of contractual, quantum meruit, negligence and statutory compensation claims following wrongful FMD slaughter and cleansing operations.
enrichment.outcome: Illegality and sham defences rejected; NCF entitled to sue on the contracts; liability established on signed timesheets and agreed July 2001 works; negligence liability for polytunnel and gate damage; deadstock compensation claim succeeded; fence-post damage claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Contracts entered by a company managed by an undischarged bankrupt are not unenforceable for public policy where section 15 CDDA preserves company liability; agreements labelled with NCF were not shams as against Defra, and after-acquired property under section 307 does not capture income-type C&D payments.
legal_issues: Whether C&D contracts were illegal because Mr Hill breached CDDA section 11
Whether agreements with NCF were shams concealing personal contracts with Mr Hill
Whether unsigned timesheets defeated contractual or quantum meruit claims
Title to sue for damage to tenant's fixtures and whether trustee's section 307 notice captured compensation
linked_authorities: Re Market Wizard Systems (UK) Ltd [1998] 2 BCLC 282
Archbolds (Freightage) Ltd v S Spanglett Ltd [1961] 1 QB 374
Shaw v Groom [1970] 2 QB 504

confidence.notes: Liability findings are detailed though quantum on several heads was reserved by earlier case management order.

notes: Working Time Regulations appeal; Kigass and List Design overruled on sick leave holiday pay.

enrichment.short_title: Inland Revenue v Ainsworth: no holiday pay accrual during long-term sick leave
key_facts: Five appeals concerned Civil Service and other employees on long-term sick leave seeking holiday pay under the Working Time Regulations after sick pay entitlement expired.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal in Kigass had held workers accrue four weeks' annual leave regardless of attendance; List Design allowed enforcement via unauthorised deductions claims under the Employment Rights Act.
The Inland Revenue appealed as interested party seeking to overrule both decisions.
Mrs Khan claimed during employment; four other appellants claimed compensation under regulation 14 on termination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeals with EAT permission against decisions following Kigass Aero Components Ltd v Brown and List Design Group Ltd v Douglas.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; Kigass and List Design held wrongly decided; no entitlement to annual leave under regulation 13 while on long-term sick leave absent working time, with consistent construction of regulation 14; holiday pay claims must be brought under regulation 30 not section 23 ERA.
enrichment.ratio: Annual leave under regulation 13 naturally means release from work obligations and serves health and safety purposes, so an employee absent on long-term sick leave without working time is not entitled to four weeks' leave or payment; regulation 14 compensation depends on regulation 13 entitlement and enforcement is exclusively under regulation 30.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 13 accrues annual leave during total long-term sickness absence
Whether regulation 14 payment in lieu applies on termination after sickness absence
Whether Working Time holiday pay can be claimed as unauthorised deduction under ERA Part II
Proper construction of leave in light of the Working Time Directive health and safety purpose
linked_authorities: Kigass Aero Components Limited v Brown [2002] ICR 697
List Design Group Limited v Douglas [2002] ICR 686
Canada Life Ltd v Gray [2004] ICR 673

confidence.notes: Central statutory construction issues and disposals on both Kigass and List Design points are fully reasoned.

notes: Attorney-General reference; blank-firing gun conversion sentences increased from six to nine years.

enrichment.short_title: Herbert and Beard: unduly lenient firearms conspiracy sentences increased
key_facts: Herbert and Beard pleaded guilty on the first day of trial to three conspiracies over ten months to manufacture, sell and possess prohibited converted firearms from blank-firing handguns.
They sourced hundreds of blank guns and ammunition from Target Arms and Moderne Buckles, converted them at Mountacre Close and stored them at Rivets Close for supply to criminals.
The judge gave full credit for late guilty pleas and imposed concurrent six-year sentences on each count from a stated nine-year starting point.
The Attorney-General referred the sentences as unduly lenient given the scale of at least 150 converted weapons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney-General reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 treated as the hearing of the reference.
enrichment.outcome: Reference granted; total sentence increased from six to nine years, achieved by three consecutive three-year terms on each conspiracy count to reflect overall criminality while honouring promised plea discount.
enrichment.ratio: Where separate statutory conspiracies cover manufacture, sale and possession of prohibited weapons in a massive gun-making enterprise, consecutive sentences may be required to mark total criminality even if concurrent sentences might suffice for overlapping conduct; full discount for very late guilty pleas in strong cases may still leave the overall term unduly lenient.
legal_issues: Whether concurrent six-year sentences were unduly lenient for hundreds of converted firearms
Whether the three conspiracy counts should attract consecutive sentences
Appropriate discount for guilty pleas entered on the first day of trial after 15 months
Application of R v Avis sentencing guidance for firearms offences
linked_authorities: R v Avis [1998] 2 Cr App R(S) 178
R v Newton 77 Cr App R 13

confidence.notes: Aggravating features, starting point analysis and substituted sentence structure are clearly explained.

notes: Election expenses declaration appeal allowed; honest examination sufficient despite agent's failings.

enrichment.short_title: Sharma v DPP: candidate's honest expense declaration not knowingly false
key_facts: Dr Dev Sharma, successful Labour candidate in a 2002 Redbridge bye-election, was convicted of knowingly making a false section 82 declaration that he had examined his agent's £630 expenses return.
The agent's return wrongly stated all bills were paid when a £600 printer's bill was paid four months later; the agent was also convicted.
Dr Sharma credibly said he trusted his agent, checked only that total spending was within the £700 limit, and flicked through two of six pages believing the return complete.
The district judge found insufficient examination but accepted Dr Sharma was a man of honesty and integrity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Thames Magistrates' Court conviction for illegal practice under sections 82(6) and 170.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; answer to case stated question is no; conviction quashed because Dr Sharma honestly believed the return complete and accurate after examination.
enrichment.ratio: Section 82(6) requires knowing falsity, not negligence; a candidate's duty is distinct from the agent's and honest belief after some examination of the return is a complete defence even if the agent was dishonest, following Jones v Whicher.
legal_issues: Whether a candidate must audit the agent's return to detect dishonesty
Whether flicking through the return constituted examination under section 82
Mens rea for knowingly making a false declaration under section 82(6)
Distinction between corrupt practice and illegal practice under section 170
linked_authorities: Jones v Whicher [1999] 2 Crim App R 253

confidence.notes: Findings of honesty, statutory mens rea analysis and distinction from agent liability are clearly articulated.

notes: War risks total loss trial; claim dismissed for wilful misconduct and material non-disclosure.

enrichment.short_title: North Star Shipping v Sphere Drake: war risks claim defeated by scuttling and non-disclosure
key_facts: The bulk carrier North Star was damaged by an underwater explosion at Drapetsona near Piraeus in July 1994 while undergoing repairs; owners claimed constructive total loss under war risks policies.
The vessel was managed by Kent Trading, beneficially owned by Harry and Michael Petrakakos, who faced Greek criminal proceedings and Panamanian fraud allegations not disclosed to underwriters.
The policy was overvalued by about US$1 million and prior premium default had led to cancellation of an earlier policy.
The court found the loss attributable to owners' wilful misconduct and that leading underwriters were induced to write cover by non-disclosure of material facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of war risks insurance claim for constructive total loss following explosion at repair berth.
enrichment.outcome: Owners' claim dismissed; insurers entitled to avoid the policy for material non-disclosure and the loss held attributable to wilful misconduct of the owners.
enrichment.ratio: Non-disclosure of Greek criminal proceedings, Panamanian fraud allegations, overvaluation and prior premium default would probably have deterred war risks underwriters on moral hazard grounds; combined with proof that the explosion was caused by owners' wilful misconduct, the assured cannot recover under the policy.
legal_issues: Whether the explosion constituted wilful misconduct by the owners
Whether Greek criminal proceedings and bail were material facts for war risks placement
Whether Panamanian fraud allegations and overvaluation induced underwriters
Whether prior policy cancellation for premium default was materially non-disclosed

confidence.notes: Conclusion on dual grounds is explicit though the very long judgment contains extensive fact-finding on scuttling not fully summarised here.

notes: British citizenship claim struck out; no arguable right by descent or registration.

enrichment.short_title: Harrison v Home Secretary: British citizenship claim struck out

statutes_considered.title: British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act 1914

key_facts: Peter Harrison, born in New Zealand in 1946, sought declarations that he is a British citizen by descent from his father born in South Australia in 1897, or entitled to registration following refused applications in 1976 and 1987.
Extensive prior litigation included failed naturalisation, judicial review, libel claims and Lewison J's rejection of an alleged ship-birth theory.
The Secretary of State applied to strike out the claim; Mr Harrison did not attend the adjourned hearing.
Harrison became a New Zealand citizen on independence and never acquired CUKC status or right of abode; registration refusals were discretionary and time-barred for judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Strike-out/summary judgment application in Chancery proceedings for declarations of British citizenship or entitlement to registration.
enrichment.outcome: Claim form and particulars struck out; no arguable claim to citizenship by operation of law; registration challenges are abuse of process and proper remedy would be judicial review, which would fail on delay and merits.
enrichment.ratio: A New Zealand-born Commonwealth citizen whose father was born in Australia did not become a CUKC under the 1948 Act and has no right of abode; refused registration decisions under the 1948 and 1981 Acts must be challenged by judicial review not declaratory proceedings, and repeated relitigation after Lewison J is an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether Harrison is a British citizen by descent from a father born in pre-federation South Australia
Whether 1976 and 1987 registration refusals were unlawful
Whether declaratory proceedings are appropriate instead of judicial review
Whether prior ship-birth proceedings preclude renewed citizenship claims
linked_authorities: Harrison v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 432
O'Reilly v Mackman [1983] 2 AC 237
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Nationality analysis and strike-out reasoning are comprehensive though the claimant did not appear at the hearing.
